name: Incident Response
description: Preparing for, detecting, containing, eradicating and recovering from security incidents, and learning from them.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-61: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
SANS Digital Forensics and Incident Response

questions.question: In the NIST incident response lifecycle (SP 800-61), which phase comes first?
options: Detection and Analysis
Containment, Eradication and Recovery
Preparation
Post-Incident Activity
questions.explanation: Preparation (plans, tools, training, contacts) comes before Detection and Analysis; containment and post-incident activity follow.

questions.question: What is the main goal of the containment step?
options: To limit the spread and damage of the incident
To permanently delete all logs
To publicly announce the attacker's identity
To restore every system from backup immediately
questions.explanation: Containment stops the incident from spreading or causing further harm while preserving the ability to investigate.

questions.question: A single laptop shows signs of active ransomware encryption. What is the best immediate action?
options: Ignore it until the next business day
Pay the ransom right away
Wipe and reimage the laptop before anyone looks at it
Isolate the laptop from the network (e.g. EDR network isolation) and escalate per the IR plan
questions.explanation: Network isolation stops spread to shares and other hosts while keeping the system available for evidence collection.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a post-incident 'lessons learned' review?
options: To assign personal blame to the analyst on duty
To identify what worked and what failed so processes, detections and controls can be improved
To close the ticket as quickly as possible
To delete evidence that is no longer needed
questions.explanation: Lessons-learned reviews are blameless improvement exercises that feed back into preparation and detection.

questions.question: Why should responders usually avoid immediately reimaging a compromised server?
options: Volatile and disk evidence needed to understand scope, root cause and persistence would be destroyed
Reimaging is illegal in most jurisdictions
Reimaging always spreads the malware to other servers
Compromised servers cannot be reimaged
questions.explanation: Without evidence, responders cannot determine how the attacker got in or what else is affected, risking reinfection.

questions.question: During eradication after a phishing-driven email account compromise, which action is most essential to prevent the attacker regaining access?
options: Changing the company's email domain name
Resetting the account's credentials, revoking active sessions and tokens, and removing malicious mailbox rules
Deleting the original phishing email only
Disabling antivirus to speed up recovery
questions.explanation: Attackers often persist through existing session tokens and forwarding rules; resetting credentials alone is not enough without revoking sessions and removing persistence.

practical.title: Draft a containment plan
practical.instructions: An EDR alert shows workstation WS-042 running malware that beacons to 198.51.100.23 every 60 seconds. In 3-6 sentences, write the containment and initial response steps you would take, in order.
practical.expected_output: Isolate WS-042 from the network, block the C2 indicator 198.51.100.23 at firewall/DNS/proxy, preserve evidence (memory and disk image) before cleaning, scope the incident by hunting for other hosts contacting the IP in SIEM/EDR, and reset potentially exposed credentials.

rubric.hint: First isolate WS-042 from the network to stop the beaconing and spread.
Block 198.51.100.23 at the firewall, proxy or DNS.
Capture memory and a disk image before cleaning the host.

rubric.description: Scopes the incident across other hosts
rubric.hint: Search SIEM/EDR for other hosts communicating with the same IP to determine scope.
Reset credentials that may have been exposed on the workstation.

tasks.title: Study the incident response lifecycle
tasks.description: Read NIST SP 800-61 and summarize each lifecycle phase with two concrete activities. Note how incidents are prioritized.
tasks.completion_criteria: A summary of all phases with at least two activities each and the prioritization factors.

tasks.title: Map an incident to ATT&CK
tasks.description: Read a public incident write-up and map each attacker action to a MITRE ATT&CK tactic and technique. Identify where detection could have happened earlier.
tasks.completion_criteria: A table mapping at least 6 attacker actions to ATT&CK techniques with a detection opportunity for each.

tasks.title: Write an incident response playbook
tasks.description: Create a step-by-step playbook for one scenario such as phishing account compromise or ransomware, covering triage, containment, eradication, recovery and communication.
tasks.completion_criteria: A playbook with defined roles, decision points, evidence to collect and a communications checklist.

tasks.title: Run a tabletop exercise
tasks.description: Design and facilitate a tabletop exercise with peers using your playbook and a realistic scenario with injects. Capture decisions, gaps and an after-action report.
tasks.completion_criteria: A scenario with at least five injects, participant decision log, and an after-action report with prioritized improvements.
